About the position

A three-year PhD position is available at the Gjærevoll Centre for Biodiversity Foresight Analyses at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU). The position is funded by NTNU Energy and also linked to the VISTA Centre for Norwegian Transformative Energy Policy Development (NOTRAP). The PhD project will explore the societally relevant intersection of biodiversity modelling, renewable energy and social-ecological systems.

We are seeking a motivated candidate with experience and interest in biodiversity science, spatial ecology, landscape ecology, land use, or other closely related topics.

The Gjærevoll Centre will be the candidate's primary workplace. Here, the candidate will be part of a dynamic and interdisciplinary research environment and contribute to the NOTRAP centre. The candidate is also expected to contribute to NTNU Energy's activities upon request.

As a PhD Candidate with us, you will work to achieve your doctorate, and at the same time gain valuable experience that qualifies you for a further career in higher education and research, in and outside academia.

Your immediate leader will be the Director of the Gjærevoll Centre.

About the project

Holistic efforts to address climate change and biodiversity loss are needed. A major research objective today is to inform a transition to renewable energy that protects areas of high biodiversity value, and the diverse and irreplaceable values nature holds for human society. This work is strengthened by a community-engaged research framework.

The Gjærevoll Centre brings together researchers from the natural sciences, mathematics and statistics, informatics, environmental engineering, economics and the social sciences to understand how biodiversity is affected by human use of land and water. By combining ecological field studies, biodiversity modelling and foresight analyses with perspectives on societal values and governance, the centre aims to produce knowledge and tools that can inform policies and actions to halt biodiversity loss.

The NOTRAP centre contributes to this aim with a focus on the nexus of energy transition and democracy, establishing Energy Policy Incubators for the co-construction of transformative energy policies. Within the PhD project, it is expected that the candidate will link assessment of biodiversity impacts of energy transition pathways with perceived importance of natural habitats by local populations. The position is funded under NTNU Energy's Focus Area 1, The Renewable Revolution. NTNU Energy is NTNU's strategic research area on energy and aims to strengthen energy research that contributes to securing climate-friendly, nature-friendly and fair energy.

The PhD project will investigate synergies between biodiversity value and societal value in areas with contested land or water use related to the energy transition. As an integrative project, it may combine approaches such as ecological fieldwork, biodiversity modelling, participatory and citizen-based mapping of biodiversity and societal values, and social-ecological systems analysis. The candidate will work with the NOTRAP centre to identify and develop links to its activities, including the Energy Policy Incubators.

The main supervisor will be Researcher Irja Ida Ratikainen (Gjærevoll Centre, NTNU). The candidate will have an interdisciplinary supervision team with co-supervisors from the Faculty of Natural Sciences, the Faculty of Engineering and the Faculty of Social and Educational Sciences.

Duties of the position

Complete the doctoral education until obtaining a doctorate
Conduct high-quality research within the framework described above
Produce a high-quality PhD thesis, comprising manuscripts suitable for publication in international peer-reviewed journals
Disseminate research results to academic and non-academic audiences
Participate actively in relevant research groups at the Gjærevoll Centre and the NOTRAP centre
Contribute to NTNU Energy's activities
Participate in international activities such as conferences and/or research stays at foreign institutions
Be prepared for changes to your work duties after employment.

Required selection criteria

You must meet the requirements for admission to the faculty's Doctoral Programme. In particular, your previous education must be equivalent to a five-year Norwegian degree programme. Your degree must include a major independent project (minimum 30 ECTS) equivalent to a master's thesis. This corresponds to an undergraduate Bachelor degree and typically a 2-year Master's degree.
You must have a strong and relevant academic background from your previous studies and have an average grade from your Master's degree study, or equivalent education, which is equal to B or better compared to NTNU's grading scale. If you do not have letter grades from previous studies, you must have an equally good academic foundation. If you have a weaker academic background, you may be considered if you can document that you are exceptionally suited for a PhD education, for example through relevant work experience and/or peer-reviewed academic works.
Documented quantitative and computational skills in general, and preferably within spatial data analysis and biodiversity modelling
You must have a Master's degree in ecology or a closely related scientific field.
Good oral and written communication and presentation skills in English.
Applicants who are about to complete their Master's degree may apply, but the degree must be completed and documented before the start of employment.

The appointment is to be made in accordance with NTNUs guidelines for recruitment positions for general criteria for the position.

Preferred selection criteria

A solid understanding of biodiversity, spatial ecology, and/or nature conservation and management
Experience from nature management, conservation practice, or participatory and community-engaged research
Experience from interdisciplinary research
Good oral and written communication skills in Norwegian or another Scandinavian language is an advantage
Personal characteristics
To complete a doctoral degree (PhD), it is important that you are able to:

Work independently and in a structured way, set goals and make plans to achieve them
Collaborate well and contribute actively to an interdisciplinary research environment
Communicate well, and present and discuss your research with other professionals and with stakeholders
Learn new methods and approaches, and adjust the plan for the project as needed
Show curiosity and a strong motivation for the research
Emphasis will be placed on personal qualities.

We offer

An exciting job with an important mission in society
Developing tasks in a strong and international professional environment
Career guidance and follow-up during the PhD period
Open and inclusive working environment with committed colleagues
Working capital that can be used to implement the project
Mentor programme as a new employee at NTNU
Favorable terms as a member of the Norwegian Public Service Pension Fund (SPK)
Free Norwegian language training at a basic level (A2)
As a PhD Candidate at NTNU, you will have access to employee benefits.

Diversity

Diversity is a strength, and at NTNU we aim to be an employer that reflects the diversity in society and that makes use of the potential of the population's collective skills. Our vision is Knowledge for a better world and our values are creative, critical, constructive and respectful. We believe that an organization that is equal, diverse and gender-balanced is essential for us to achieve our goals.

We strive to attract employees with different skills, life experiences and perspectives to contribute to even better problem solving of our societal mission in research and education.

If you think this position is relevant and interesting, we encourage you to apply, regardless of gender, functional ability and cultural background, or whether you have been out of work for a period of time.

Salary and conditions

In the position of PhD Candidate, code 1017, your gross salary will normally be NOK 580 000,-per annum depending on qualifications and seniority. A 2% statutory contribution to the State Pension Fund is deducted from the salary.

The employment period is 3 years.

For employment as a PhD Candidate, it is a prerequisite that you gain admission to the PhD programme in Biology within three months of your employment contract start date, and that you participate in an organized doctoral programme through out the period of employment.

As an employee at NTNU, it is important that you keep yourself up to date with academic and organizational changes and adapt to them.

For the necessary professional and social interaction, it is a prerequisite that you are physically present and available to the institution on a daily basis.

The appointment is carried out in accordance with the principles of the State Employees Act, and Export control (legislation that regulates the export of knowledge, technology and services). Candidates who, after assessment of the application and attachments, are considered to bein conflict with the criteria in the latter act, will not be able to be employed.

About the application

The attachments (idetailed below) must accompany the application as these documents form the basis of the application assessment. The cover letter and CV must be in English or Norwegian/a Scandinavian language.

Please note: the application will only be assessed on the basis of the information we have received by the application deadline. Therefore, make sure that your application clearly shows how your skills and experience meet the criteria described above. The application and all attachments must be sent electronically via Jobbnorge.no. If you are invited to an interview, you must bring certified copies of certificates and diplomas upon request.

The application must include:

A cover letter (maximum 1 page) explaining your motivation for applying, how your background meets the selection criteria, and which research questions or approaches within the scope of the position you would be interested in developing
Curriculum Vitae (CV)
Transcripts and diplomas for Bachelor's and Master's degrees
Your Master's thesis. If you have recently submitted your Master's thesis, you can attach a draft of the thesis. Documentation of a completed Master's degree must be presented before taking up the position.
Any publications other relevant research work
Names and contact information of three relevant referees

If all, or parts, of your education has been taken abroad, we also ask you to attach documentation of the scope and quality of your entire education, both Bachelor's and Master's education, in addition to other higher education. If your institution uses “diploma supplement” (normal for most European institutions), you must attach this. A description of the documentation required can also be found here. If you already have a statement from Norwegian Directorate for Higher Education and Skills (HK-dir), please attach this as well.

Joint work will be considered. If it is difficult to identify your contribution to joint work, you must attach a brief description of your participation.

When assessing the best qualified, we emphasize necessary qualifications such as education, experience and personal suitability. Motivation for the position, ambitions, and potential for research will also count when assessing the candidates.

NTNU recognizes a wide range of academic contributions and has committed itself to The San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment and CoARA (responsible assessment of research and recognition of a greater breadth of academic contributions in accordance with NTNU's social mission).

General information

A public list of applicants with name, age, job title and municipality of residence is prepared after the application deadline. If you wish to be exempt from entry on the public applicant list, this must be justified. Assessment will be made in accordance with current legislation. You will be notified if the exemption is not granted.

If you think this position looks interesting and in line with your qualifications, you are welcome to apply.

If you have any questions about the position, please contact Researcher Irja Ida Ratikainen, email: [email removed]

If you have any questions about the recruitment process, please contact HR Consultant Gerd Flataas, email: [email removed]

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: The overall aims of the research projects are to generate scientific information on improving fresh produce safety. Current projects include characterization, prevention, and mitigation of foodborne pathogen survival and persistence on fresh produce and in the processing environments. Under the guidance of a mentor, you will have the opportunity to be involved in the following research areas: 1) Assessing and improving fresh produce postharvest washing, packing, and storage practices; 2) Multi-species biofilm characterization and mitigation; and 3) Control of Cyclospora at pre- and post-harvest environment in fresh produce production, and 4) Improving the detection of foodborne pathogens. Assessing and mitigating risks of foodborne pathogens in controlled environment agriculture (CEA) systems. Conventional microbiological, advanced molecular biological, and multi-omics approaches will be applied. You will also collaborate on other research projects aimed at improving fresh produce safety.

Gain experience collaborating with mentors and team leaders to design scientific studies and develop research plans.
Build skills in executing studies according to established protocols and adapting research plans as needed based on emerging findings or operational considerations.
Develop proficiency in collecting, managing, and analyzing data to test hypotheses and draw preliminary conclusions.
Strengthen scientific communication skills by collaborating closely with mentors and team leaders to interpret, document, and report research findings.

Research Project: This opportunity, available at the USDA Agricultural Research Service in the Food Systems Research Unit in Burlington, VT, focuses on characterizing long-term phenology of perennial pasturelands of the Northeastern US, using remote sensing tools, and understanding drivers and impacts of phenological changes among the ecoregion. You will collaborate closely with food systems modelers, agronomists, GIS specialists, and animal scientists, and will gain the ability to collect and combine existing productivity, geospatial, land use, and other economic, and environmental datasets to investigate regional opportunities and trends.

EPA Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention (OCSPP), located in Durham, North Carolina. You will receive training in the Research Triangle Park, NC campus.

The mission of EPA is to protect human health and the environment. EPA works to ensure that: Americans have clean air, land and water; National efforts to reduce environmental risks are based on the best available scientific information; Federal laws protecting human health and the environment are administered and enforced fairly, effectively and as Congress intended; Environmental stewardship is integral to U.S. policies concerning natural resources, human health, economic growth, energy, transportation, agriculture, industry, and international trade, and these factors are similarly considered in establishing environmental policy; All parts of society have access to accurate information sufficient to effectively participate in managing human health and environmental risks; Contaminated lands and toxic sites are cleaned up; and chemicals in the marketplace are reviewed for safety.

Research Project: You will gain experience in data management and analysis across coordinated research and informatics efforts focused on advancing developmental neurotoxicity (DNT) risk assessment and related regulatory science capabilities. These projects encompass a range of data science activities needed to analyze toxicological data, including maintaining models, productionizing research endpoints, developing R packages, and supporting software development, database curation, and quality evaluation efforts for in vitro chemical screening data. Research activities may include acquiring domain knowledge in toxicology and chemistry to support data analysis; wrangling heterogeneous source formats into standard templates for processing; conducting data analysis and curation using controlled vocabularies; performing database scripting; managing code libraries and documentation; identifying and correcting bugs as part of quality control; conducting user acceptance testing; developing automated tools for processing large volumes of data; and applying innovative data science solutions to support risk assessment and regulatory decision-making.

Other research activities may include:
Being a part of an interdisciplinary team of developers and scientists 
Creating data visualizations to communicate results to stakeholders
Thoroughly documenting all research activities as directed by EPA mentor to comply with EPA quality assurance procedures for transparency and reproducibility
Drafting reports describing complex datasets or data manipulation procedures
Presenting research in internal reports/memos to be used by EPA scientists
You may have the opportunity to present research at scientific conferences or contribute to scientific manuscripts 
Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will learn how to: 

Design and implement reusable and scalable techniques for data management
Organize or transform data in databases to support scientific analyses 
Analyze data quality according to specified criteria
Write scripts and functions in R to support data migration and data curation software tools
Develop and collaborate with others to evolve scientific applications into production level tools

Description
Veterinary Post Doctoral Position

We seek a recently qualified veterinarian that has a specific interest in wildlife research to undertake a variety of studies and complement our existing research efforts. We require the incumbent to contribute to current projects by undertaking a variety of wildlife immobilisations in addition to his / her research activities. We would like the veterinarian to develop his / own research projects within the context of ABEERU. Two projects that we envisage initiating that have a specific wildlife veterinary flavour include: 

1.      Health, Morphology and Population Genetics of Black-backed Jackals and Brown Hyaenas reliant on Vulture supplementary sites

Vulture restaurants (VRs) are established primarily to provide predictable, uncontaminated food resources for vultures. However, the long-term provision of concentrated food subsidies may also influence other scavenging mammals that exploit these resources. Where a VR has operated continuously for several decades, it provides a unique opportunity to investigate the ecological and biological consequences of sustained anthropogenic food supplementation.

This project will investigate the long-term effects of a VR that has been operational for over 30 years and where domestic livestock carcasses (specifically domestic pigs) have historically constituted the dominant food resource. The study will focus on two important mammalian scavengers, the black-backed jackal (Lupulella mesomelas) and brown hyaena (Parahyaena brunnea). 

The central premise is that prolonged access to an abundant and predictable anthropogenic food subsidy may influence these species at multiple biological levels. 

The overall aim will be to determine whether long-term access to a concentrated anthropogenic food subsidy has influenced the nutritional and physiological health, morphology, relatedness and population genetic structure of the black-backed jackal and brown hyaena population proximate to the VR.

The study will:

Assess nutritional and physiological health 
Characterise morphological variation 
Determine relatedness among individuals 
Assess genetic diversity and population genetic structure 
Integrate physiological, morphological and genetic data

The project addresses an important but poorly understood consequence of wildlife supplementary feeding. While VRs are generally established for conservation purposes, their ecological effects may extend beyond their intended target species. 

The findings will have direct relevance for the management of VRs and other supplementary feeding programmes. They will help determine whether such interventions have unintended consequences for non-target species, including changes in nutritional condition, body morphology, population structure, relatedness and genetic diversity. The project therefore provides a strong interdisciplinary platform for a veterinary postdoctoral researcher while contributing to broader questions concerning wildlife health, conservation management and the ecological consequences of anthropogenic resource subsidies.

2.  Do nature reserves act as reservoirs for damage causing animals in farmlands?

The focus of this study is to use molecular techniques to understand the relatedness between black-backed jackals and caracals in conservation areas to black-backed jackals and caracals on farmlands. The genetic material from damage causing animals will be derived from culled animals on farmlands. The veterinarian will capture animals in conservation areas and collect genetic material to compare to material from culled animals. 

The aim of this study is to establish the relatedness between damage causing animals on farmlands and those in conservation areas. This will allow us to determine whether conservation areas act as source populations that contribute animals that prey on livestock. 

Requirements

A BVSc degree with a specialisation in wildlife veterinary practice, obtained within the past five years. 
Demonstrable experience in wildlife related veterinary practice, including the chemical capture of free roaming (not exclusively zoo or captive animals) wild animals (preferably including a spectrum of species). 
An interest in wildlife veterinary research. 
A track record of peer-reviewed scientific publications and conference presentations relevant to wildlife research. 
The ability to work independently and collaboratively within a multidisciplinary research team. 
Willingness and ability to travel to various field sites to undertake and oversee fieldwork and data collection.
International applicants should be aware that they will need to apply for the necessary equivalence certifications from the South African Veterinary Council so that they can operate unsupervised in South Africa.

Description
Postdoctoral Research Fellowship Vegetation ecology & soil post doc 

We invite applications from early-career terrestrial vegetation ecologists for a three-year Postdoctoral Fellowship within the Applied Behavioural Ecology & Ecosystem Research Unit (ABEERU), Department of Environmental Sciences, University of South Africa (UNISA).

The successful candidate should have a strong background in vegetation ecological research, with additional experience in soil chemistry and soil microbial activity. The position offers an opportunity to contribute to existing interdisciplinary research projects while developing an independent research profile within the broad field of vegetation ecology.

Research projects

The postdoctoral fellow will contribute to existing research projects, including the following:

1. Ecological effects of megafaunal carcass decomposition in savanna ecosystems

We plan to initiate a broad-spectrum study investigating the immediate and longer-term ecological effects of large mammal carcass decomposition in a savanna ecosystem, potentially at Madikwe or Timbavati. The study will use elephant carcasses originating from management culling operations or sanctioned commercial hunts, subject to the necessary permissions and approvals.

Carcass decomposition represents a potentially important source of nutrients and organic matter, with the capacity to influence soil properties, microbial activity and vegetation dynamics. However, the extent, duration and spatial distribution of these effects, particularly following the decomposition of very large mammals, require further investigation.

The study will investigate ecological responses across a range of parameters, with a particular emphasis on changes in soil chemistry, soil microbial activity and vegetation composition and structure. The successful candidate will contribute to the development of the research design, field data collection, laboratory analyses and interpretation of the results, with the opportunity to develop specific research questions within this broader project.

2. Long-term studies of bush encroachment management in Highveld grasslands

ABEERU is involved in long-term research investigating the effectiveness of different management treatments for addressing bush encroachment and changes in grassland composition. Particular attention is given to Stoebe vulgaris and its effects on grassland vegetation.

These studies provide opportunities to investigate vegetation responses to management interventions over time, including changes in species composition, plant diversity and vegetation structure. The successful candidate will assist with the continued monitoring and analysis of these long-term experiments and contribute to evaluating the ecological outcomes of different management approaches.

3. Long-term monitoring of grazing lawns

The Unit is also involved in long-term monitoring of grazing lawns, providing opportunities to investigate vegetation dynamics and changes in plant community composition under sustained grazing pressure.

The successful candidate will contribute to ongoing monitoring and data analysis, with the potential to investigate relationships between vegetation composition, plant diversity and grazing-related changes in grassland and savanna ecosystems.

Independent research development

In addition to contributing to existing projects, the successful candidate will be encouraged to develop an independent research project within the broader field of vegetation ecology, particularly vegetation classification, plant diversity and vegetation dynamics.

EPA Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), located in Durham, North Carolina. 

The mission of EPA is to protect human health and the environment. EPA works to ensure that: Americans have clean air, land and water; National efforts to reduce environmental risks are based on the best available scientific information; Federal laws protecting human health and the environment are administered and enforced fairly, effectively and as Congress intended; Environmental stewardship is integral to U.S. policies concerning natural resources, human health, economic growth, energy, transportation, agriculture, industry, and international trade, and these factors are similarly considered in establishing environmental policy; All parts of society have access to accurate information sufficient to effectively participate in managing human health and environmental risks; Contaminated lands and toxic sites are cleaned up; and chemicals in the marketplace are reviewed for safety.

Research Project: With thousands of commercial chemicals entering the environment, traditional animal-reliant safety assessments can no longer keep pace with the demand for rapid hazard and exposure data. To bridge this gap, EPA’s Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention is pioneering in vitro 'New Approach Method' (NAM) testing strategies to enable fast, cost-effective screening, prioritization, and human health risk assessments. This specific internship is deeply anchored within the analytical chemistry foundation necessary to validate and drive these alternative strategies forward.

As an intern on our team, you will gain experience with EPA’s Risk Assessment Support Division by learning about analytical chemistry method development, validation, and execution. Your primary learning objective will be designing robust sample preparation and quantitative analysis procedures to track chemical concentrations and stability within complex in vitro and biochemical assay matrices, specifically targeted at biological perturbations such as endocrine disruption.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will learn to operate and troubleshoot advanced instrumentation, utilizing high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) and liquid/gas chromatography (LC-MS/MS, GC-MS/MS) to generate high-quality, reproducible kinetic profiles. By pairing your rigorous analytical measurements with exposure-dose and toxicokinetic modeling, you will directly enable the team to translate laboratory data into 'equivalent doses,' allowing scientists to compare systemic configurations against anticipated exposure levels to evaluate overall risk (hazard + exposure = risk).

Learning objectives include:

Advanced Method Development & Validation: Gain hands-on experience in designing, optimizing, and validating highly sensitive, selective analytical chemistry methods to extract and quantify trace-level organic chemicals across diverse and challenging biological and cell-culture matrices.
High-Throughput Analytical Instrumentation: Master the operation, calibration, and troubleshooting of advanced instrumentation, including ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with triple-quadrupole and high-resolution mass spectrometers (UHPLC-MS/MS, Q-TOF).
In Vitro Toxicokinetics (IVTK) Characterization: Develop proficiency in calculating chemical parameters, including hepatic metabolic clearance rates, plasma/media protein binding, and chemical stability, which are vital for determining points of departure for endocrine disruption pathways.
Data Analysis Automation & Quality Assurance: Learn to implement automated data processing pipelines for mass spectrometry datasets, apply rigorous QA/QC metrics, and maintain strict data integrity practices matching good laboratory practices (GLP).
Regulatory Integration & Cross-Disciplinary Teamwork: Understand how raw analytical chemistry data directly translates through exposure models to shape EPA screening, prioritization, and toxicological policy decisions, while enhancing collaborative communication across chemical and biological domains.

Experience with automated sample preparation systems, solvent evaporation units, homogenizers, centrifuges, HPLC, GC, mass spectrometry, and wet chemistry techniques

As the Nation's largest water, earth, and biological science and civilian mapping agency, USGS collects, monitors, analyzes, and provides science about natural resource conditions, issues, and problems. 

Additional information about research happening at EESC can be found at: Eastern Ecological Science Center | U.S. Geological Survey

Research Project: The USGS Eastern Ecological Science Center is searching for a highly motivated fellow interested in turning high throughput sequencing amplicon datasets generated from environmental DNA (eDNA) collected from various ocean habitats into interpretable biomonitoring data that describe “who is there”, and how these communities differ temporally and spatially.

This fellowship will provide an opportunity to learn how existing bioinformatic pipelines are developed, evaluated, improved, and applied to eDNA datasets from diverse marine environments for analyzing eDNA datasets from ongoing projects in the Gulf of America and the Aleutian Basin, as well as other marine environments as project objectives continue to expand. The general analytical approach is referred to as “eDNA metabarcoding”. Data analysis activities will include processing raw sequencing runs of multiple metabarcoding markers into amplicon sequence variant tables using custom scripts and open-source statistical analyses and visualization software like R. Under the guidance of a mentor, you will gain experience collaborating with federal, academic, and Tribal partners who are interested in integrating eDNA results with other environmental monitoring data. among federal, academic and tribal partners where these groups will be interested in integrating the eDNA results with other monitoring and experimental data collected concurrent with eDNA samples such as water column nutrients, benthic infauna, ocean currents, coral density, etc. 

You will have ample opportunity to gain hands-on experience with data that will help address conservation challenges facing marine ecosystems, contribute to peer-reviewed publications, interact with scientists from other USGS science centers as well as other federal agencies, and to build up their bioinformatic capabilities.

Learn how environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding is used to characterize marine biodiversity and determine how biological communities vary across locations and time.
Gain experience processing high-throughput sequencing data from marine environmental samples into amplicon sequence variant (ASV) tables.
Learn to develop and improve bioinformatic pipelines for analyzing eDNA datasets from the Gulf of America, Aleutian Basin, and other marine environments.
Build skills in custom scripting, open-source bioinformatics tools, statistical analysis, and data visualization in R.
Learn to integrate eDNA metabarcoding results with complementary ocean-monitoring data, such as nutrient levels, benthic infauna, ocean currents, and coral density.
Gain experience applying bioinformatic and biomonitoring data to marine-conservation questions and ecosystem-management challenges.

Research Project: This research project will develop and validate components of the EPA developmental neurotoxicity (DNT) in vitro battery, a suite of new approach methods (NAMs) designed to evaluate chemicals for potential adverse effects on the developing nervous system. The DNT in vitro battery offers a path forward by combining complementary cell-based assays that capture key neurodevelopmental processes, including neuronal proliferation, migration, synaptogenesis, and network activity, into a tiered, mechanistically-informed testing framework. Building confidence in this battery requires rigorous assay development, robust data analysis, cross-agency collaboration, and linkage of in vitro endpoints to apical outcomes and regulatory points of departure. 

The objective of this research project is to advance the scientific credibility and regulatory utility of the DNT in vitro battery through integrated wet lab and bioinformatic approaches. You will contribute to assay development and optimization, perform comparative analyses of new and historical datasets, evaluate assay transferability across partner agencies, and conduct predictive analyses linking in vitro endpoints to apical toxicological outcomes. Under the guidance of a mentor, you will synthesize findings for peer-reviewed publication and stakeholder communication. Research activities may include, but are not limited to:

Hands-on participation in the development and optimization of in vitro assays comprising the DNT battery
Bioinformatic analysis of assay data, including integration and comparison with existing historical datasets
Collaboration with partner agencies to evaluate the transferability and reproducibility of DNT battery assays across laboratories
Statistical and computational analyses to identify which assays are most predictive of apical neurotoxicity outcomes and regulatory points of departure
Reading and interpreting relevant scientific literature on developmental neurotoxicity, NAMs, and regulatory toxicology
Active participation in meetings of the project team, branch, and division
Preparing reports, presentations, and summaries of research findings
Opportunity to present research at professional and regulatory science meetings
Authoring or co-authoring manuscripts for publication in peer-reviewed journals
Learning Objectives: Through participation in this opportunity, you will learn how to:

Perform and optimize key in vitro assays within the DNT battery, including cell culture techniques and endpoint measurement
Apply bioinformatic tools and workflows to analyze high-content screening data and compare results across datasets and laboratories
Evaluate assay transferability and interlaboratory variability in the context of test method validation and regulatory acceptance
Use statistical approaches to assess the predictivity of in vitro endpoints relative to apical neurotoxicity outcomes and existing points of departure
Integrate findings across multiple lines of evidence to build scientific confidence in a NAM-based testing battery
Communicate complex scientific results to both technical and regulatory audiences through written reports and oral presentations

Learn more about being a member of Team WDFW!


WDFW’s Fish Ageing and Otolith Laboratories provide critical age and origin data to WDFW Fish Management and Hatchery Divisions, tribal co-managers, and federal fisheries managers to be used in forecasting, run reconstruction, stock assessment, and scientific research.

With your expertise in the preparation and processing of calcified structures, you will conduct research and report on biological studies of Pacific Salmon and other marine, anadromous, and freshwater fishes.

Your work as part of the Otolith Laboratory Team will directly support efforts to meet resource and economic needs for the State of Washington and the Pacific Northwest, including programs focused on recovering Endangered Species Act (ESA) sensitive stocks.


What to Expect:
Among the varied range of responsibilities held within this role, the Otolith Laboratory Biologist’s duties will include,

Thermal Mark Implementation and Evaluation:
Prepare high-quality, half-sectioned and thin-sectioned otolith samples.
Use lapping wheels for grinding and polishing.
Communicate effectively with lab team members and supervisor to ensure accuracy and meet project deadlines.
Independently observe otoliths using compound and dissecting microscopes to identify and decode thermal marks.
Accurately records thermal mark information into database.
Review and plan distinctive thermal mark patterns aligned with hatchery requests.
Develop thermal marking schedules.
Coordinate, adapt, and communicate hatchery thermal marking schedules to achieve intended thermal marks.

Microstructural and Microchemical Analyses:
Prepare high-quality samples from otoliths and other calcified structures for microstructural and microchemical analyses using low-speed saws and lapping wheels.
Use image analysis software and microscopes to measure and count daily increments in otoliths to evaluate environmental, ecological, and anthropogenic influences on growth during early life history.
Evaluate and summarize results of daily growth estimates, accuracy and precision of estimates, size-at-marine entry, and other relevant parameters.

Data Collection, Analysis, and Reporting:
Perform statistical analysis and interpretation of data.
Prepare reports, peer-reviewed publications, and presentations at conferences and other meetings.

Assisting and Supporting Production, Thermal Marking Operations, and Field Collections:
Assist hatchery and lab staff with artificially spawning and cross-fertilizing salmonid gametes.
Travel to study sites to assist with or lead collection efforts for biological samples.

 Working Conditions:

Work Setting, including hazards: Work primarily occurs in a laboratory setting, but will also include office environments, hatcheries, and field sites. Perform repetitive fine motor functions for long durations. Extended periods of time will be spent looking at computer monitors or through microscopes.

Laboratory hazards include hot surfaces (hot plates, burners), grinding wheels, sharp blades, dissecting tools, and chemical exposure (acids, ethanol, acetone, thermoplastic resin, and polystyrene resin) both direct and as fumes.

Hatchery and field work may be performed during inclement weather and over slippery, uneven terrain near or on the water. Lift equipment, samples, coolers, and field gear weighing up to 75 pounds, with assistance as needed. Travel will include operating, or being a passenger in, a motor vehicle on highways or dirt roads. This position may involve working in or near water, including tasks that require navigating, negotiating, and performing duties related to water environments.

Schedule: Typically, Monday–Friday, 8:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m. The work schedule may require weekend work or extended hours while in the field.

Travel Requirements: Occasional field work, laboratory work, and projects will require travel throughout Washington state. Attend annual workshops and conferences. Travel may include overnight and day trips. Increased travel potential November–February.

Tools and Equipment: Compound and dissecting (stereo) microscopes, epifluorescence microscope, desktop/laptop computers, image analysis software, dissecting tools, precision grinders, hot plates, fume hood, balances, and low-speed precision saws will be used routinely. Portable chilling units and pumps will occasionally be set up and maintained for hatchery production or controlled experiments.

Customer Interactions: Public interactions are uncommon but may occur when entering state buildings, working at hatcheries, or conducting fieldwork. Collaborate and professionally communicate with Tribal/First Nation groups and co-managers, WDFW staff throughout the state, non-profit organizations, academic groups, public utilities, federal agencies, other Washington state resource agencies, and fisheries agencies from other states.


Qualifications:

Closely related qualifying experience may be substituted for the required education on a year-by-year basis.

Required Qualifications:

Option 1:
A Bachelor's degree in fisheries, biology, natural resource science, environmental science, or a related field.
  AND
Three (3) years of professional experience in fish research or management.

Option 2:
Two (2) years as a Fish & Wildlife Biologist 2.


In addition to meeting one of the options listed above, the following are also required and may be gained concurrently:

One (1) year of experience with the following:
Processing or analyzing calcified structures.
Producing high-quality otolith sections, including preparing and analyzing otoliths for thermal mark interrogations, microstructure, and/or microchemistry analysis.
Reading and interpreting multiple band otolith patterns, including reading/evaluating calcified structures for age estimation or thermal mark patterns.

Ability to:
Accurately perform repetitive motions utilizing fine motor skills for long periods of time.
Prepare 20-40 otolith thin sections and 50-100 otolith half sections daily.
Read 100-300 otolith samples daily.

Knowledge of:
Pacific salmon life history and growth.


Please Note:
A Master’s degree in the applicable science may substitute for one (1) year of the required experience in fish research or management.
A Ph.D. in the applicable science may substitute for two (2) years of the required experience in fish research or management.

 Certifications/Licenses:
Valid Driver’s License.


Preferred Qualifications:
In addition to the required qualifications, our ideal applicant will possess some or all the following:

Master’s degree in a relevant biological science.
Authorship or co-authorship of one (1) or more peer-reviewed publications.

Experience:
Processing and analyzing data obtained from otoliths or other calcified structures.
Applying current fish ageing research methods.
Enumerating daily growth increments in otoliths.
Otolith thermal mark identification.
With, or knowledge of, Pacific Northwest fish biology and ecology, including life history and population dynamics.
Managing multiple complex projects with competing deadlines, producing accurate and timely work.
Analyzing data to evaluate issues, assess options, draw conclusions, and support decision-making.
Defining research questions, identifying data needs, and designing independent experiments.

Learn more about being a member of Team WDFW!


As the Ballast Water Vessel Inspector, you’ll help protect Washington’s waters from aquatic invasive species and support the long-term health of our marine ecosystems.

In this role, you’ll train to conduct onboard inspections of commercial vessels arriving in Washington State to ensure compliance with ballast water management regulations designed to prevent the spread of invasive species. You’ll work in active port environments throughout the Strait of Juan de Fuca, mid-Puget Sound, including Seattle and Everett, and north Puget Sound up to the Canadian border.

This is a great opportunity for someone interested in maritime operations, environmental compliance, vessel inspection, and protecting Washington’s natural resources through hands-on fieldwork and regulatory enforcement.


What to Expect:
Among the varied range of responsibilities held within this role, the Ballast Water Vessel Inspector will,

Vessel Ballast Water Risk Audits:
Assess daily vessel arrivals to identify the highest ballast water risks using vessel compliance history, department protocols, and professional judgement.
Select, board, and inspect at least 5% of all targeted vessel arrivals in assigned region.
Explain state laws and regulations and assist vessel officers and crew in meeting compliance objectives for state ballast water management.
Complete required department inspection forms per protocols.

Compliance Actions:
Assess onboard evidence of ballast water management compliance using vessel records, equipment specifications, and certifications.
Investigate and issue appropriate compliance actions per department protocols for vessel situations including Warnings, Notice of Corrections, or recommendations for Notice of Penalty.
Compile evidence to create professional and legally defensible compliance actions.

Coordination, Planning, and Reporting:
Coordinate with the U.S. Coast Guard and Department of Ecology to support cooperative vessel management and minimize duplication of efforts on concurrent vessel boardings.
Analyze, evaluate, and interpret vessel inspection data.
Assist senior staff in writing annual and biennial compliance, accomplishment, and recommendation reports.
Support the development and implementation of work plans, regulatory updates, performance measures, management forms, protocols, and procedures. 
Participate in state, regional, and national work groups as assigned.

Monitoring and Research:
Conduct onboard testing of new protocols and equipment as directed.
Analyze ballast water treatment system (BWTS) voyage maintenance records and annual independent laboratory performance test reports to support the development of new regulatory requirements.
Assist senior staff in developing and evaluating enhanced vessel ballast water and biofouling risk assessment protocols.
Develop, evaluate, and interpret protocols, tools, and performance measures used to assess the effectiveness of ballast water management practices.

Work Setting, including hazards: Work is performed in potentially hazardous industrial port environments aboard merchant vessels conducting cargo operations. Board and inspect all types of vessels in a variety of weather conditions and physically access all areas of vessels, including climbing ladders and entering engine/pump rooms, and occasionally, ballast tanks to inspect ballast management activities. Frequently lift and carry a 40-pound gear bag. Handle hazardous biological sample preservation chemicals, such as Formalin and ethanol. This position may involve working in or near water, including tasks that require navigating, negotiating, and performing duties related to water environments.

Schedule: This position is full-time, working 40 hours per week. The standard work schedule includes the potential for occasional evening or weekend work as needed. Schedules may vary based on business needs, time of year, and/or weather conditions.

Travel Requirements: Travel between state ports is required and may average approximately 1,500 to 3,000 miles per month.

Tools and Equipment: Use appropriate safety equipment including flotation devices, hard hats, safety goggles, and steel-toed boots. 

Customer Interactions: Regular interaction with regulated industry representatives, including situations that may be complex or confrontational. Communication may also involve working with individuals for whom English is a secondary language.

Marine Engineering
Nautical Industrial Science
Naval Architecture
A closely related field

Environmental Planning
Marine Engineering
Natural Sciences
Nautical Industrial Science
Naval Architecture

*Two (2) years of professional-level experience in vessel design or vessel inspection.

Shipping regulatory and management operations.
Vessel operations.
Vessel and port safety requirements.

Marine and freshwater Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) risks to the state, including ballast water and biofouling pathways and management techniques.

Position/Project Specifics:

The Ecosystem GIS and Data Specialist supports the Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission (PSMFC) Habitat Program by assisting with data stewardship, geospatial analysis, scientific visualization, and data communications efforts. Description
 Painted Bunting Field Technician – Georgia Coast 
 Overview: 
The University of Georgia’s (UGA) Rushing Population Ecology Lab is seeking 1 field technician to assist with research on Painted Bunting (Passerina ciris) migration and resource use ecology at Wormsloe in Savannah, Georgia. The technician will work full-time at UGA’s Center for Research and Education at Wormsloe independently and serve as the point person for work at the site. The technician will work remotely alongside a PhD student (who is primarily located 2 hours away) and assist with all aspects of fieldwork. 
 Primary fieldwork responsibilities include: 
Catching and banding birds using baited traps and mist nets
Removing pressure geolocator tags from birds
Possibly applying fixed loop geolocator tags on birds 
Collecting and storing fecal samples from birds
Conducting avian point counts
Inputting and proofing data

Secondary responsibilities may include: 
Tracking birds using handheld radio telemetry
Outreach to the public
Assisting with other ongoing research at site (including but not limited to: archaeology, bat movement ecology, native plant gardening, etc.)

Daily monitoring activities may include transporting field equipment in summer heat, humidity, wind, rain, and buggy conditions. Successful applicants will be experienced bird banders and be able to make good decisions/ adapt on the fly. Successful applicants will also have an interest in avian ecology, strong work ethic, eagerness to learn and help, positive attitude, effective communication skills, and a willingness to work in harsh field conditions.

This position provides exciting opportunities to learn new skills and collaborate with conservation professionals on the Georgia Coast while advancing the candidate’s career goals. The technician will reside at UGA’s Center for Research and Education at Wormsloe outside of Savannah, Georgia (accessible by car). UGA’s Center for Research and Education at Wormsloe has an active interdisciplinary research program (especially with bat ecology and archaeology) with graduate researchers and UGA classes cycling through the site throughout the summer. Successful applicants will have strong interpersonal skills and a curiosity for all facets of research at the site. Preference will be given to applicants with passerine banding, handling, and tagging experience. Shared, on-site housing is provided.

Deadline: Applications will be reviewed as received so please apply as soon as possible; deadline 12/06/2026 (or until filled)
Dates: April 12 – June 18 (start and end dates flexible; move-in date 1-2 days before start date)
Pay: $16/hour, 40 hours/week for 10 weeks

Please email a 1-page cover letter, resume, and the names/contact information of 3 professional references in a single PDF. Name this file with "Your_Last_Name_PABU_Tech.pdf" and send to Diane Klement ([email removed]) with "Your_Last_Name_PABU_Tech" in the subject line of the email by the deadline. Please include the number of birds that you have extracted from mist nets and banded and your experience with tagging. Applications will be reviewed as they are received, so please apply at your earliest convenience.

Description

Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission is recruiting candidates to fill the role of a Fishery Biologist 2 located in La Grange, California. This is a full-time, benefits-eligible position with an anticipated start date of January 11th, 2027.
 
In the first year, the biologist will lead the development of a comprehensive Spring‑run Chinook Salmon life cycle monitoring plan, integrating field methods, analytical approaches, and adaptive management strategies to support basin‑wide conservation goals. In the second year, the biologist will oversee a team of technicians to implement the monitoring plan, ensuring high‑quality data collection and consistent field operations across diverse habitats. This role is ideal for candidates who thrive in both outdoor fieldwork and data‑driven scientific analysis, and who are motivated by meaningful environmental stewardship.
 
Essential Functions:  Included in this band are professional positions that perform recurring assignments ranging from moderate difficulty where conventional or straight-forward biological concerns are encountered to complex assignments where specialized knowledge and demonstrated competence in advanced techniques are required.  (The functions listed below are characteristic of the type and level of work associated with this group and pay band.  They are not all-inclusive. Individual positions may perform some or all, as well as other similar work.) 
At the lower end of the range, Fishery Biologists have a solid working knowledge of established scientific methods and techniques to perform recurring assignments of moderate difficulty.  Methods and techniques are well established, apply to most situations, and do not require significant deviations.  Resource planning reports generated by employees at this level involve conventional biological concerns.  Reports generated may be short-range management plans or portions of annual work plans.  Lower range work examples include:
Develop age composition structures, stock assessments, escapement totals, harvest levels, run reconstruction frameworks, and/or run forecasts for designated fish species and stock. Evaluate and direct sampling efforts or reporting practices to best meet data requirements. Write memoranda and reports necessary for transfer of information to the appropriate individuals, agencies, and organizations.
Plan, design, schedule, and conduct fish catch and effort surveys for marine fisheries. Utilize existing general creel survey protocols and determine modifications that address specific marine fisheries conditions or special fisheries. Work with state, federal and regional fishery management councils to provide data on fisheries catch and effort and population trends as well as biology of marine fish species. Work with stock assessment biologists in relation to fisheries-specific data utilized in their stock assessments. Assist with database presentations of the data collected. Prepare reports and presentations as requested. Provide expertise in improvements to the design of creel surveys

Position/Project Details:
European green crabs are a recently established marine invader on the west coast of North America. Currently, resource managers rely on trapping and molt surveys for biosurveillance and early detection. Environmental DNA (eDNA) offers a promising additional tool for early detection of green crab, but its use is currently limited. This is largely because guidance on designing effective eDNA surveys and translating survey results to management actions is lacking.

The overall research objective is to develop and refine eDNA methods to complement other early detection approaches and increase the capacity of current biosurveillance programs. This includes identifying eDNA sampling strategies that maximize detection probabilities, applying these findings to the design of effective green crab eDNA surveys, and clarifying how survey results should be interpreted for practical decision making.

Because green crabs, as hard‑shelled crustaceans, shed relatively little eDNA and inhabit diverse and dynamic environments, foundational studies on effective eDNA sampling strategies are needed to advance the method. The incumbent uses eDNA and modeling approaches to evaluate green crab densities and trap catch-per-unit-efforts, environmental effects, spatial sampling strategies, and sampling effort and is open to other relevant considerations. In addition, the incumbent may be involved in DNA-based studies that evaluate the effectiveness of light traps or other methods for capturing green crab larvae for early detection.

Description
Position Overview

We are seeking a skilled and passionate Wildlife Biotechnology & Biobanking Technician to join our Memphis Zoo Conservation and Research team to work in reproductive technologies and molecular biology to advance wildlife conservation.

As a core member of our lab, you will managing our biomaterial repository (biobank), conducting biobanking and reproductive research, and assisting with processing and extraction and processing samples for routine molecular assays for qPCR disease testing and enzyme immunoassay. This position reports directly to the Senior Conservation Biologist and offers a unique opportunity to apply cutting-edge biotechnology directly to endangered species preservation.

Essential Job Functions:
Assist with planning and execution of conservation and biobanking research projects, for biobanking genetics of Southeastern endangered snakes and other species as well as coordinate opportunistic biobanking collections during routine physicals exams and post-mortem gamete rescue.
Assist with in situ conservation and research efforts, that may include multi-day trips to Louisiana, Florida, and Mississippi to collect samples from wild-collected snakes for biobanking, data curation and processing, etc.
Assist with ex situ conservation and research efforts, including assisting with monitoring animals for captive-breeding efforts, through disease testing, hormone monitoring, and ultrasound.
 Key Responsibilities
Biobanking & Repository Management
Preserve and catalog diverse biological samples (e.g., tissue, blood, gametes, and cells) from wildlife species.
Maintain cryopreservation equipment (liquid nitrogen tanks, ultra-low freezers) and manage digital inventory database systems.
Ensure strict adherence to quality control, biosafety protocols, and sample tracking standards.
Travel with researchers for collection and biobanking samples at other Zoos and facilities
Reproductive Research & Biotechnology
Support assisted reproductive technology (ART) research, including semen collection techniques, semen analysis, gamete processing, and cryopreservation protocols.
Prepare media, reagents, and specialized equipment for reproductive physiology experiments.
Assist in endocrine monitoring initiatives by performing routine fecal hormone extractions and enzyme immunoassays (EIAs).
Monitor and document experimental outcomes with high precision.
Molecular Biology Support
Perform routine DNA/RNA extractions from a variety of challenging wildlife tissue types.
Run qPCR/PCR assays for disease screening for heard/colony health monitoring and conservation initiatives
Laboratory Operations & Collaboration
Maintain a clean, organized, and safe laboratory environment in coordination with the Lab Manager.
Work with lab manager to maintain laboratory instrumentation.
Collaborate with multidisciplinary teams, including veterinarians, animal care teams, and external conservation partners.
Assist with preparations of permit applications and reports.
Contribute to scientific manuscripts.
Mentor students and volunteers.
Foster a positive, collaborative, safe, and encouraging professional environment.
Perform various duties as assigned.

Qualifications & Skills
Required:

Education: Bachelor’s degree in Biology, Wildlife Science, Molecular Biology, Reproductive Physiology, Animal Science or a closely related field.
Experience: Minimum of 1–2 years of hands-on laboratory experience (academic or professional).

Technical Skills:
Strong record of use and knowledge of reproductive biology techniques (e.g., microscopy, gamete handling) 
Experience with semen analysis (including CASA, flow cytometry, staining techniques) and cryopreservation technique 
Experience with basic lab techniques and equipment 
Familiarity with sterile techniques and basic liquid handling.

Attributes: 
Exceptional organizational skills, meticulous record-keeping, and a strong commitment to wildlife conservation.
 Record of effectively communicating conservation and research efforts, goals, and accomplishments to the public.
 Record of peer-reviewed publications and/or conference presentations.
 Proficient in MS office suite and R or other programs for statistical analysis 

Preferred:
Master’s degree in Biology, Wildlife Science, Molecular Biology, Reproductive Physiology, Animal Science or a closely related field.
Knowledge of reproductive biology techniques (e.g., microscopy, gamete handling).
Familiarity with computer assisted sperm analysis (CASA).
Experience with immunoassays and sample extractions.
Experience with DNA/RNA extraction and qPCR/PCR setup

Supervisory Responsibility: Students, interns, and volunteers may be the supervisory responsibility of this position.

The noise level in the work environment is usually quiet while in the office, or moderately loud while on Zoo grounds.

GIS and Cartography Support Members, Midwest Regional Office


Summary
American Conservation Experience, a nonprofit Conservation Corps, in partnership with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS), is seeking 4 Member(s) to contribute to GIS and cartography projects under the mentorship of U.S. Fish and Wildlife (USFWS) Staff.


For more information about ACE, please visit our website.


Start Date: January 2026 (flexible)
Estimated End Date: January (with possibility of extension)
*a 52 week minimum commitment is required, approximately 2080 hours*


Location Details/Description:  Midwest Regional Office -Bloomington, MN

The Midwest Region of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service provides leadership and administrative support for wildlife conservation efforts across Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Ohio and Wisconsin. It coordinates programs related to ecological services, refuges, fisheries, migratory birds, land acquisition and management, ensuring consistent delivery of the agency’s conservation mission throughout the Midwest.
For more information about the midwest region, please visit the FWS website.

Position Overview: The mission of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) is working with others to conserve, protect, and enhance fish, wildlife, plants, and their habitats for the continuing benefit of the American people. This position will help FWS realize that mission at the midwest regional office.


Members will support cartographers and other USFWS staff with the creation, management, and analysis of geospatial data through the use of GIS, remote sensing, and cartographic techniques. It involves working with staff and producing accurate maps, maintaining geospatial databases, and collaborating with technical staff to support a wide range of spatial data needs and field operations.


Specific duties include: 

Convert historical and contemporary spatial records into digital geodatabases.
Scan, georeference, and digitize maps, imagery, and other geospatial source materials.
Delineate and reconcile geographic features and boundaries using GIS tools.
Conduct quality control and quality assurance on geospatial datasets.
Produce digital and hardcopy maps for technical, management, and field-use audiences.
Collect spatial and environmental data using standardized field and GIS procedures.
Manage, store, and organize spatial and field data within databases or spreadsheet systems.
Create cartographic products for field operations, presentations, and publications.
Communicate GIS, remote sensing, and cartographic concepts to colleagues and technical partners.
Maintain effective working relationships with project leads, management, and technical staff.
Perform GIS data creation, editing, and attribute management to support cartographic workflows.


This individual placement is meant to facilitate professional development and promotes exposure to land management agencies and networking with professionals. This could include gaining experience in different conservation fields and shadowing different work groups.


Schedule:Duties will typically be carried out between 8:00am and 4:30pm Central, Monday - Friday, typically 5 days/week (5/8s). Work hours may vary. Bi-weekly totals should not exceed 80 hours. A flexible work schedule may be required, which could involve work performed outside of normal work hours including on weekends and/or holidays. Time off may be granted and requests should be directed to ACE and the FWS for approval.



Position Benefits


Living Allowance: The ACE Member is expected to contribute ~40 hours/week and will receive a living allowance of $1030/week to offset the costs of food and incidental expenses, dispersed bi-weekly.


Public Land Corps Hiring Authority: Members serving under this agreement may be eligible for a federal hiring authority upon completion of their term of service and 640 hours of service. If the duration of a PLC-eligible term is not long enough for Members to accrue 640 hours of service (~16 weeks), the total hours served at the completion of the term may be eligible to be combined with hours accrued from another PLC-eligible term to meet the 640 hours requirement. PLC projects also include specific eligibility requirements such as age and citizenship. Please contact ACE staff with questions about eligibility, or view general eligibility information on our website.


Housing: Housing is the responsibility of the member and not provided by ACE or FWS.


Gear Reimbursement: ACE members will have up to $200 to spend on eligible gear purchases. Eligible gear for this position includes office attire, boots, socks, pants, outerwear, personal office supplies, etc., and must be approved by ACE staff prior to purchase. 


Provided Training/Orientation: ACE members will receive position specific training and an orientation outlining ACE policies and procedures, clear guidance on prohibited activities, and networks for support. Specific training may include broader Service requirements along with GIS and cartography skills such as additional mapping applications, data management standards, and enhanced imagery or remote-sensing interpretation.



Qualifications 


Required:

Members must be authorized to work in the United States. ACE does not provide sponsorship for employment visas. 
Willing and able to represent ACE and the partner organization in a professional, positive, and enthusiastic manner. 
Ability to be both self-directed/work alone, and be a positive, contributing member of a group.
A valid driver's license and an insurable driving record (documentation to be provided upon request). Members must be 21+ to drive due to ACE’s insurance and liability requirements.
Willing to undergo and must pass the required criminal history checks 
Ability to perform the essential duties of the position with or without reasonable accommodation.
ACE Members will need to complete bi-weekly timesheets, beginning of term feedback forms, end of term evaluations and for longer terms, a mid-term evaluation. 
Member may not participate in any prohibited activities as listed in the Member Service Agreement.
To learn more about eligibility requirements, please visit our website. 

Preferred:

Competitive applicants for this position can hold a minimum of a Bachelor’s or Master’s degree and/or have relevant experience in subject areas such as ArcGIS Online, ArcPro, geospatial data management, remote sensing.
Ability and willingness to think critically and problem solve.
Good organizational skills (documenting processes, data management, and file management).
Good communication skills (ability to summarize complex geospatial information orally and in writing, ability to effectively communicate with staff and partners from an interdisciplinary background and with different levels of management experience). 
Proficiency in ArcPro and AGOL to create and maintain GIS data in accordance with federal requirements.




Physical Demands, Work Environment and Working Conditions: 

Physical Demands: Manual dexterity required for use of computer keyboard/mouse and other office equipment.
Vision Requirements: Requires close, distance, peripheral and depth perception vision as well as the ability to focus. 
Weight Lifted or Force Exerted: Frequently moves up to 5 lbs., ability to move up to 10 pounds.
Environmental: Mainly indoor, office environment conditions; indoor air quality is good and temperature is controlled.
Noise Environment: Moderate noise such as in a business office with equipment and light traffic.
Travel: This position may require domestic travel.

Environmental Conditions/Hazards:  The ACE member(s) may encounter environmental conditions/hazards including extreme heat or cold, rocky terrain, swamp or wetland conditions, biting insects, and potentially dangerous wildlife. The member is expected to conduct duties in a safe and orderly manner so as not to endanger self, fellow staff/members or resources.

Vehicle and Equipment Use/Safety: If a vehicle is required for the accomplishment of the duties, one will be provided by the FWS or ACE.  Any tools required for the accomplishment of the duties will be provided by the FWS. Use of personal protective equipment (PPE), typically provided by the FWS, will be mandatory for any activity that requires it.  Strict adherence to FWS and ACE equipment training, certification and safety protocols is required.  

To Apply: Please submit your resume, a cover letter demonstrating your interest and experience, and contact information for three professional/academic references to ACE’s online application page for this position on our website.Early consideration will be given as applications are received. This position may close at any time. If you have any questions regarding this position please feel free to contact ACE EPIC FWS Program Manager, Johannah McCollum.


If you meet at least 70 percent of the qualifications, we want to hear from you!

ACE participates in E-Verify and will provide the federal government with your Form I-9 information when you are enrolled in a program to confirm that you are authorized to work in the U.S.

EEO:  Employment or Service with ACE is based upon ability, qualifications, attitude, and job-related factors. Every qualified employee, member, or applicant has the same opportunity for recruitment, hire, training, transfer, promotion, compensation, demotion, termination, benefits, employee activities, and general treatment without regard to race, color, religion, age, sex, creed, national origin, pregnancy, ancestry, citizenship status, genetic information, veteran or military status, physical or mental disability, sexual orientation, medical condition, marital or parental status, political affiliation, ethnicity, hair texture or style, arrest record, caste, hereditary status, endogamy, or any other classification protected by applicable local, state, or federal law.

Contact
Johannah McCollum

TPWD MISSION


To manage and conserve the natural and cultural resources of Texas and to provide hunting, fishing and outdoor recreation opportunities for the use and enjoyment of present and future generations.

GENERAL DESCRIPTION:


Under the direction of the Hatchery Biologist, this position performs fish and wildlife conservation work and is responsible for assisting in propagation, rearing and distribution of fish species. Monitors and records water quality.  Performs data collection duties and accurately records fish samples. Responsible for grounds, facilities, and equipment maintenance. Completes routine administrative paperwork. Performs additional duties as assigned. Complies with all Agency and Division rules, regulations and procedures.


Note: 


Selection as a Fish and Wildlife Technician III requires at least 5 years of experience as a TPWD Fish and Wildlife Technician II and ability to perform additional advanced duties and responsibilities. For posted positions, this experience must be included in the job history on the application to be considered.


 


MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS:


Education: 


Graduation from High School or GED.


Experience:


FWT IA: No experience required.


FWT IB: Two years of relevant experience


FWT Il: Four years of relevant experience. 


FWT III: Five years of experience as a TPWD Fish and Wildlife Technician II and capable of performing significant additional duties/responsibilities as described in FWT III Essential Job Functions and KSAs.


Licensure:        


Must possess or be able to obtain, within 30 days of employment, a valid class 'C' Texas driver's license.


Must possess or able to obtain, within 30 days of employment, a Hunters Safety Education Card.


NOTE: Retention of position contingent upon obtaining and maintaining required license.


 


ACCEPTABLE SUBSTITUTIONS:


Education: 


FWT IB and II ONLY: Graduation from an accredited college or university with a relevant advanced degree (Bachelor's, Master's, or PhD) may substitute for two years of relevant experience.


 


PREFERRED QUALIFICATIONS:


Education:       


Graduation from an accredited college or university with a Bachelor's degree in Fisheries Science or related biological science.


 


KNOWLEDGE, SKILLS AND ABILITIES:


Fish and Wildlife Technician I


Knowledge of fish and aquatic organisms.


Knowledge of vehicle and motor mechanics, maintenance, and operation. 


Fish and Wildlife Technician II


Knowledge of FWT I; PLUS


Knowledge in the principles of fish husbandry and aquaculture.


Knowledge of potential environmental contaminants and fish kills.


Knowledge of division and agency policies and procedures.


Fish and Wildlife Technician III


Knowledge of FWT II; PLUS


Knowledge of department purchasing and operating procedures.


Knowledge of environmental regulations and procedures pertaining to hatchery operations.


Fish and Wildlife Technician I


Skill in effective verbal and written communication.


Skill in engaging with the public and teammates in a polite and professional manner.


Skill in demonstrating good work habits.


Skill in using MS Word, Excel and Outlook.


Fish and Wildlife Technician II


Skills of a FWT I; PLUS


Skill in handling high pressure situations.


Skill in identifying freshwater fishes, plants and organisms.


Skill in designing, maintaining and repairing specialized hatchery equipment.


Skill in making independent, sound, timely decisions.


Fish and Wildlife Technician III


Skills of FWT II; PLUS


Skill in working as an effective and efficient team member and/or leader.


Skill in training others.


Skill in understanding and optimizing water quality parameters and recognizing data anomalies.


Skill in using analytical equipment and explaining functionality to others.


Fish and Wildlife Technician I


Ability to accurately follow written and verbal instructions.


Ability to work as a member of a team.


Ability to perform manual labor including, lifting supplies and materials up to 50 lbs.


Ability to conduct work activities in accordance with TPWD safety program.


Ability to operate light farm equipment and pull a gooseneck trailer (within 3 months of hiring).


Fish and Wildlife Technician II


Ability of a FWT I; PLUS


Ability to work independently with little or no supervision.


Ability to maintain facilities and equipment.


Ability to identify fish disease and stress.


Fish and Wildlife Technician III


Abilities of a FWT II; PLUS


Ability to convey the mission to a diverse audience.


Ability to train less tenured technicians.


Ability to work effectively with co-workers and representatives from external organizations and the public.


Ability to work under limited supervision, with moderate latitude for the use of initiative and independent judgment.

Required to work 40 hours per week, includes flexible schedules with hours other than 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. and days off other than Saturdays, Sundays and holidays as necessary.


Required to work overtime as necessary.


Required to perform work outdoors, in adverse weather conditions.


Required to perform work in water-based field activities, including work aboard boats.


Required to perform manual labor including, lifting supplies and materials up to 50 lbs.


Required to operate a state vehicle.


Required to travel 10% with possible overnight stays.


Must conform to TPWD dress and grooming standards, work rules and safety procedures.


Non-smoking environment in State buildings, common areas, boats, and vehicles.

Provides technical assistance and public outreach programs to the general public, private landowners/land managers, sportsmen, and new constituencies. Disseminates information to the general public through news releases, radio/TV interviews, program presentations, and other public outreach and educational opportunities. Education:
Graduation from an accredited college or university with a Bachelor's degree preferably in Wildlife Science, Wildlife Management, Wildlife Ecology, Range and Wildlife Management, or closely related field in Natural Resources Management. Experience:
NRS I: No experience required.
NRS II: Two years of relevant experience.
NRS III: Six years of relevant experience.

must possess or be able to obtain, within 30 days of employment, a valid State driver's license.
